mcqs.question: A message protected only by a single parity bit gets corrupted in exactly 2 bit positions during transmission. What happens when the receiver checks parity?
options: The parity check correctly flags the corruption every time
The parity check passes even though the data is corrupted — two flips cancel out and parity looks unchanged
The receiver automatically corrects both flipped bits
Parity checks are undefined for more than one bit error
mcqs.explanation: A single parity bit only tracks whether the total number of 1s is even or odd; two bit flips change two bits' values but leave the overall parity unchanged, so the check passes despite real corruption — parity's well-known blind spot to even numbers of errors. Parity alone never corrects errors, only (partially) detects them.

mcqs.question: A code has a minimum Hamming distance of 5 between any two valid codewords. How many bit errors can it correct?
options: It can only detect errors, never correct them, regardless of distance
mcqs.explanation: The correction capability formula is floor((d_min - 1)/2); with d_min=5, that's floor(4/2) = 2 correctable bit errors. It can detect up to d_min-1 = 4 errors, but detection and correction have different bounds, and correction is possible whenever the minimum distance is large enough relative to the number of errors.
